utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Also good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you, too. Any preliminaries before we --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Before the witness comes in and proceeds with his testimony, we have an oral decision on the matter related to the scheduled or proposed interview by the OTP of Defence witness Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley. This is an oral decision. Of course I have written points, and we'll try to get through it as quickly as we can, so as not to take much time from this witness's testimony. The Trial Chamber is seized of the following matter. On the 30th of November, 2005, the Defence filed an extremely urgent motion for an order regarding an authorised prosecutorial contact with a witness in light of information it had received from the Prosecution or from the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case that the Prosecution had scheduled an interview with Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley, a Defence witness. On the same date, 30th November, the Trial Chamber issued its order on extremely urgent Defence motion, ordering the Prosecution to postpone its scheduled interview until such time as the matter could be addressed in the next court -- during the next court sitting, the next scheduled court sitting. On the 2nd of December, the Prosecution filed its response to the Defence motion, and on December 6th it filed a corrigendum to its response. On the 6th of December, 2005, the Defence filed its reply to the Prosecution response. In a court sitting in a sitting held yesterday, the 6th of December, both the Prosecution and the Defence provided additional oral submissions with respect to certain aspects of the Defence motion, the Prosecution response, and the other issues that arose therefrom. On the 7th of December, that's today, the Defence provided the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber with two communications from the US government, one being a letter sent by fax to them and the other being a copy of an email message in response to the Defence request contained in the annex -- in Annexes A and B of the Defence reply of the 6th of December, to which I made reference during the debate yesterday. The Trial Chamber, having discussed it amongst ourselves at length, the issues involved, firmly believe, we firmly believe, that the whole controversy between the parties rises as a result of a misunderstanding by the Prosecution of our decision on the 29th September, 2005, in which or by which we granted the application of Rule 70 to the proposed testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley. It appears to us that the Prosecution maintains or maintained that the -- our September decision authorised them, that is the OTP, to seek and obtain an interview with the said witness. We wish to make it clear that when we handed down our 29th September 2005 decision, we did not have before us as a Trial Chamber any such request from the Prosecution, nor did we deal anywhere in that decision with such a request. What is contained in that decision is a reference to the position taken by the US government in relation to the concerns shown and expressed by the Prosecution with regard to possible questions to the witness relating to credibility and on other matters not covered nor dealt with in the examination-in-chief. The understanding of the decision could and should have been that in a timely fashion the Prosecution should have communicated to the US government the other areas they wish to cross-examine the witness upon, with a view to obtaining clearance from that government, pursuant to Rule 70. Instead, on the 8th of November, 2005, that is approximately one month before this witness was scheduled to start giving his evidence, the Prosecution asked the United States government for a confirmation that the authorisation given by the USG to the OTP to interview Lieutenant Colonel Dudley a year earlier for "lead and background information," was not valid. The Defence was not made privy to this exchange of letters between the OTP and the USG. What followed was a communication by lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case to the Defence in the early evening of November 29, that the Prosecution would be interviewing Lieutenant Colonel Rex Dudley the next day. This prompted the Defence to file the extremely urgent motion that I mentioned to -- that I mentioned earlier. This was followed by this Chamber's order of the 30th November, which requested the Prosecution to reschedule the interview, to occur no earlier than yesterday, that is December 6th, as I explained earlier. The first point that we wish to make is that notwithstanding what we have just stated in regard to the September 29 decision and what should be the understanding of it, this does not in any way answer the question on the alleged irregularity of the Prosecution's request and plan to interview Lieutenant Dudley which depends on a completely separate and distinct consideration, namely the question whether one party in a case has a right to seek an interview with a proposed and declared witness of the other party. The Tribunal's Rules are silent on this matter, but over the years which Tribunal has been in existence it has become undoubted that either party has such a right. Needless to say, such right does not carry with it a corresponding duty on the part of the prospective witness to submit himself or herself to being so interviewed. The Tribunal's Rules are, naturally, also silent on how this right is to be exercised. What this Trial Chamber is, however, convinced of is that such a practice should be resorted to in a way which it's not obstructive or perversive of justice or the course of justice. What was said in Stanisic by this Trial Chamber differently presided and composed on the 6th of June of this year is very pertinent to this issue. The Trial Chamber in that case said: "Normally it is permissible for a party to interview and take statements from a witness or prospective witness, whether or not that witness has been interviewed or called as a witness by the other party. However, in seeking to interview a witness, who to the Defence's knowledge is to be called by the Prosecution, the Defence may well expose itself to the suggestion that it has improperly interfered with the witness. In order to avoid such allegations of such nature, it could be prudent for the Defence to discuss its intentions to interview a witness or potential witness with the Prosecution and to record the interview." In my opinion, this would equally apply in the inverse situation, that is when it is the OTP seeking to interview a Defence witness, as is in this case. In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, the question as to whether, in this case, the Prosecution should have informed the Defence, and when it should have informed the Defence of its intention to interview Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, has been superceded by the events and the Trial Chamber sees no utility in dwelling on this matter. This leads to the Trial Chamber -- the Trial Chamber to its first conclusion, namely that independently of its September 29th, 2005, decision, the Prosecution had a right to seek an interview with Lieutenant Dudley, a declared Defence witness. The other related question is whether there is anything in the Rules or in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal which would restrict the exercise of such right until after that the witness has been proofed by the Defence. The Trial Chamber finds that there is nothing which would support such a restriction, although in such a matter caution and reasonableness are to be recommended so as not to introduce in the trial environment an aura of distrust and mutual suspicions and accusations of foul play. In the present case the coinciding of the proposed date of the interview by the OTP of the witness with the proximity of his arrival to The Hague to start giving evidence on the December 12th is related to the date when the US government confirmed to the OTP the date when his interview could take place, although it is equally true that the Prosecution could have made their request at least a month earlier, their request to the US government. The position, however, is that the Trial Chamber cannot stop the Prosecution from interviewing this declared Defence witness, even if this takes place before he is proofed -- before his proofing by the Defence. The next issue to be decided upon is whether once this is so the Defence can insist to be present during the interview by the OTP of Lieutenant Dudley. On this matter, the position that the Trial Chamber takes is that it cannot in any way impose on the Prosecution the duty to allow the Defence to be present during the interview of Lieutenant Dudley. This remains so, even in the light of the neutral position taken by the United States government on the matter and which the Trial Chamber has been made aware of. There is, however, one overriding consideration in this matter, namely that the interviewing and future testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Dudley will be regulated by Rule 70 of this Tribunal, which, in this case, could result with the Defence not being able to know before it proofs the witness and before he starts his evidence of which other areas he will be testifying upon cross-examination that were not covered by the authorisation of the United States government to the Defence, to which the September 29th, 2005, decision refers. The Trial Chamber has a responsibility to conduct the proceedings in the best manner possible, to avoid unnecessary delays and stoppages, and in so doing the Trial Chamber firmly believes that in the situation in which this controversy arises and finds itself, it is imperative that the Prosecution undertakes to inform the Defence immediately of the additional areas that the United States government has authorised them to cross-examine the witness upon. The Trial Chamber makes it clear that it understands that Rule 70 would cover details disclosed during the interview, but this should not hinder, in any way, what is being provided and ordered by the Trial Chamber. Last but not least, the Trial Chamber makes it also clear -- also makes it clear that the interviewing of Lieutenant Dudley by the OTP should be scheduled so as not to interfere the scheduled proofing by the Defence of the said witness. For this purpose the parties are requested to cooperate between themselves. And that is our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour. There is a couple of matters. One is a matter of clarification. I always understood that Lieutenant Dudley was going to be interviewed by telephone when he was still in the States, not when he was here. We have only two and a half days or something to proof our witness. So if I am to understand from your judgement, your decision, that in fact we're going to lose even more time of that precious time because the Prosecution is going to be proofing our witness. That's one matter which I would appreciate clarification on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is a matter that, of course, we anticipated and which we discussed in camera in my chamber earlier on, and to which of course we will come as soon as we hear all the interventions. The next point?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well the other point is we seek certification of Your Honour's decision under Rule 73(B), I would say just immediately since this is urgent. Our ground would be that the decision is eviscerated by the following error, that Your Honours have not taken into consideration at all the fact which we raised in our reply that we're going to have effectively an obstruction between us and our -- the witness when we're proofing him, and that he will feel that he cannot divulge matters which were discussed with him by the Prosecution. And we now, for the first time I have to say, first time in the Defence case we're going to not be able to have a complete relationship of trust and confidence with one of our witnesses and Your Honours have not taken that into consideration nor the impact on the rights of the accused. Therefore I ask to appeal, for Your Honours to grant leave to appeal, and for a stay of execution so that we can have an appeal before this goes ahead, this interview. Your Honour, I can't stress strongly enough, this is a very important witness for us. He goes to counts -- all the counts of the indictment, including Counts 1 and 2. If we find that because of Your Honours' ruling we're not able to proof the witness in the way that we deem that we have to in the interest of our client, then we will drop that witness and we will lose an extremely important witness for the Defence. And I only wish Your Honours had taken that into consideration, the fact that this is going to have an extremely adverse impact on us. So that's my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One other matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned that a full record should be kept of the interview. I trust that that would be disclosed to us. If the Prosecution tape-records the interview, that that would be disclosed to us? Do I understand that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you follow the transcript you will notice that that is a recommendation if it is possible under Rule 70, but it is not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the United States government is happy with that then presumably Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, you deal with that. I mean, we will not go into that. I was very careful in the choice of words that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I appreciate that because we are not -- under no obligations to undertake such measures, and I see no obligations or so from the Rules to do so. And in addition to that we yesterday already stressed that we might not be able to organise it by Thursday, and yesterday in addition at the latest moment I learned that the witness will fly to Europe on Thursday, meaning that we can only try to organise it on Friday. Perhaps it can only be on Saturday. So still valid is the fall-back position, the submission that I made for an adjournment or the scheduling of this witness whenever not being dropped by the Defence, as such. And in that order -- and to support your Court, I will update and notify the Court via the Senior Legal Officer of any possibility to interview this witness in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, yes, basically we have -- yes, Mr. Jones, you wanted the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was just to react to this idea of proofing the witness on Saturday. I really don't think it can be envisaged that we start proofing this witness and we start exchanging confidential, privileged information, then he trots down the road and is interviewed by the Prosecution, then he comes back to us. Really, Your Honour, I implore you to apply some reasonableness and common sense to this. And I really think if the shoe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honours, if the shoe were on the other foot, if it were a question of the Defence requesting, and a month late because we hadn't done it on time, to interview a Prosecution witness and to take from their precious time, and I emphasise it is precious time for proofing, we feel with this witness that the two or so days we have - we're in court on Friday - is barely enough for us to be on top of this witness. First to then donate four or five hours for the Prosecution to proof is really not reasonable, Your Honour, for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, Mr. Jones, and we certainly appreciate what you have suggested. And this is why I refer you to two parts in our decision. One is that the interview by the Prosecution should not interfere with your scheduled proofing. The Trial Chamber would never dream of curtailing on your time -- the time you require to proof this witness. That's number one. And secondly, what we mentioned earlier on, it is our belief that had -- after the 29th September decision, the Prosecution could have tabled its request to the US government, either along the lines of what was discussed for the purpose of that decision, in other words to find out, get authorisation, on other areas to be covered by cross-examination; or if they chose to interview this witness, something completely different, they could -- if had they tabled that request with the US government a month before, we wouldn't have found ourselves in this predicament. So our position is this: We are granting certification. That's number one. And number two, number two, in view of the fact that we -- the way we see it, there is no way this interview can be held now in a way which would guarantee you a sufficient time to proof the witness as scheduled. We are cancelling the -- next week's entire schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have another witness next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you prepared to bring forward that and have that witness testify before Lieutenant Colonel Dudley?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would have to check whether he's available. He's -- and I should say in January he's going to the other side of the world. He has a new posting, so he's only available between now and Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's available and you want to produce him on the said dates, that is the 15th and the 16th or the 14th to the 16th, yes, of course, we will hear -- I was working on the assumption that you did not want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The sequence issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- change the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can we revisit that and get back to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. But please let us know at your earliest. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will of course support any fulfilling of the needs by the Defence to proof the witness. So it can be that it's impossible for us to have the interview prior to the proofing, but if given that impossibility we might review him after the proofing. And if that interferes with any scheduling of the witness in trial and it will be, then that will jeopardise either the trial or limit our possibility, and that's also a new development when it comes to, indeed, your consideration of the schedule of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, everyone has to live with the consequences of his own actions. This is, to a large extent, self-inflicted. Had you written to the US government a month earlier, we wouldn't have been faced with this eleventh-hour problem a couple of days before this witness was supposed to come here and give evidence. This is why I say everyone has to be reasonable and everyone is expected to live with the consequences of his own actions. Let's start with the witness. Madam Usher, can you please usher him in. Apart from the fact that we feel that the environment has been poisoned, the whole environment has been poisoned, we take strong objection to some of the words used yesterday during the intervention by Mr. Jones in particular. We cannot allow the situation to become worse because the proceedings will suffer, the trial will suffer. And we intend, actually, to find time to bring you together round the table in my chambers together with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, and we try to put some words which would try to bring us back to a healthy environment in this trial, because I am afraid it's getting from bad to worse. And the worst it gets, the more difficult it will be for us to bring this trial to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable, Mr. Smajlovic. Welcome back. I'm sorry we kept you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry we kept you waiting for three-quarters of an hour, but we were dealing with a procedural matter, not involving you in any way, which we had to deal with and decide. So we will continue with your testimony and we will proceed at the fastest rate possible. Madam Vidovic will be continuing with her examination-in-chief, and please try to follow my recommendation of yesterday to be brief in your answer. And if you can answer a question by a mere yes or no, then please do so. Thank you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will continue from where we left it off yesterday. Yesterday you testified about intense attacks against Potocari, Likari, Djogazi, Pecista, and so on in the period on and around the 8th or 9 October, 1992, up until the 14th of October, 1992. And that's where we stopped. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all I want to ask you the following: At the time these events transpired, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the area of Peciste, Djogazi, and Dugo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were you doing in the area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went over there to help the villagers of Djogazi, Peciste, and Dugo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you go over there to help? What was happening there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the area was under fierce artillery and infantry attacks from all directions, especially from the direction of Bratunac and Sase. The attacks increased in intensity all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us you knew Mr. Naser Oric. Do you recall whether he took any part in these events in this time period?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber where he was located at the time, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall very well. Naser Oric and his group from Potocari were in Potocari and at Budak.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to know this?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this because Potocari and Budak are quite close to the area where I was, Dugo Polje, Djogazi, and Peciste.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, and I'm referring to the period between the 7th or the 8th of October -- rather, let's say the 8th October, because you weren't you sure about the dates yourself, up until the 14th of October, 1992, did you have occasion to meet with Naser Oric in the area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis. We would run to each other's assistance, depending on which village came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If someone were to claim that in the period between the 5th and -- 5th and 15th of October, 1992, Naser Oric was present every day at a certain institution in Srebrenica, to your knowledge would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall -- in this particular period of time, when did you return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that it wasn't before the 14th. I remember that on that day one of my fighters, Fikret Kajevic was seriously wounded. And we took him from the area where we were towards Srebrenica. On our way, in Potocari, I met Naser, who also set off towards Srebrenica. As we were on our way, he helped us carry the wounded person, and we talked about the situation in general, including certain groups that were in Srebrenica and did not come to anybody's assistance in the general area. We were particularly angry with Hakija Meholjic, who had a 150-strong group, and still refused to help us because if the Serb forces entered Potocari that would mean that they entered Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During this particular conversation with you, did he tell you whether he ever went to Srebrenica at the time at all?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was unable to because at that time I saw him every day and we did not have a single moment of respite from the intense attacks against the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 14th of October you took the wounded person to Srebrenica. Did you return to the front line that very day or not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I returned right away. I only took some time to change my clothes and I immediately set off to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just to make it easier for us to follow, could you please ask the witness whether he could show on the map the movements he is describing, the places between which he is going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness, please, show the Trial Chamber the place on the map, the places that you mentioned. I believe they were Potocari, Djogazi, Pecista, and the other places that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, if you have a ball-point pen there with you, please use it to place your initials in the bottom right-hand corner, indicating that you made the markings.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, does that suffice? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, our last question was whether you returned to the front line immediately, and you said you did. Did you see Mr. Naser Oric that day again?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I was going through Potocari we came across each other and I went toward the villages of Pecista and Djogazi, and they set off in the direction of Budak.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move to a different topic now. Yesterday we talked about the villages of Poloznik and Pirici. Do you know the area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the time period we are concerned with, that's to say October and November 1992, were you aware of Muslim refugees hiding in the woods of Loznica and Pirici, and my question concerns the start of the war up until wintertime?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. I learnt that from the people who went in search of food in those particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that these areas, and I mean Pirici, Poloznik, and the surrounding woods where you said refugees hid, that these very refugees were target of the attacks by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that from the people who went over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you heard from them?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from people who went in search of food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber from which areas or Serb villages the Muslim refugees in the woods and the -- Pirici and Poloznik itself were attacked by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bela Crkva, Loznicka Rijeka, Kunjerac, Sase, and Andrici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to draw your attention to the transcript. I keep using in B/C/S the word "zbijeg" [phoen] which means a group of thousands of refugees, and what was entered into the transcript was merely "refugees" which does not really reflect what witness and I have been discussing. That's why I would like the word to be entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that declaration? Does it suffice, in other words, for your purposes or not, the fact that you have brought this up?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance now in showing the witness D922, Defence exhibit. This is document by the Bratunac Battalion command bearing the following number: 04337015, addressed to the commander of the Birac Brigade. I will quote the document. It's quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, it's not the --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The Birac Brigade, yes. And I quote: "Reply to your memo on the exact position of our units. Loznicka Rijeka, Kunjerac, Pobrdje, Mahmutovici," and so on. I will not be reading the names of the other villages, you have the document before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows. The document, according to what you know, does it accurately reflect the situation on the lines held by the Serb forces in the general area of Sase?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at a different document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the document be given D763, please, D763. This is a document by the Bratunac garrison command dated 11 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote the document here, witness; I believe you have it before you. "To perform preparations on lifting the line Tomica Hill-Andrici, the units which should be activated are Pobrdje company, Red Berets platoon, and Sase and detachment. The responsible person for fulfilling this task is the first-class captain Jovan Zivanovic. To perform blocking of the line Kunjerac-Kostanovice-Andrici. The units which should be activated are Mostanice company, Kostanovice first platoon, and Andrici platoon. The responsible person for fulfilling of this task are Andjelko Obrenovic and Sreten Petrovic. Perform preparations on lifting the line Zagoni-Ladja-Vresinje. The units which should be activated are Repovac platoon Hranca platoon, Seliste, police reserve unit, Slapasnica company and Magasici platoon, together with Slapasnica platoon. The responsible persons for fulfilling this task are Slobodan Ilic, Stanko Vasiljevic, and the whole command." And number 4: "Miloje Bozic is responsible for helping to perform orders and to help the organisation of the Fakovici area. Perform these tasks immediately." My question is as follows: A number of units were mentioned here, which according to this document were engaged in Sase, which is the Pobrdje company, Red Berets platoon, Mostanice company, Kostanovice first platoon, police reserve platoon, and so on. According to you -- your knowledge, were these the units attacking the surrounding Muslim villages or were those merely village guards from those villages?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the units attacking the surrounding villages, and these same units attacked the area I was at in this period of time. As I indicated earlier this was from the direction of Bratunac toward Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify this. When you say that they were attacking neighbouring villages, do you mean Serb villages or Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim villages. Pirici, Poloznik, Stozersko, Skenderovici, the Muslim part of Sikiric Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they attacked the area where you were located. How did they go about it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they started attacking with armoured mechanised units, then with fierce artillery fire, which meant that strong infantry attacks were soon to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what you observed and experienced, could these units be considered village guards?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those were well-equipped and well-trained units which had all sorts of weaponry and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness D765, please. This is a document by the Bratunac garrison command dated 13 November 1992. Daily report bearing the number 04336995. I will quote the document. "In the course of the day -- in the course of today, the attacks at Pirici and Poloznik were carried out at 9.00, inflicting great losses on the enemy. "To this moment we have received reliable information about 20 killed enemy soldiers and extensive material damage. We will submit a detailed report tomorrow because our operation is ongoing. "Yesterday on 12 November 1992, three enemy soldiers were killed in an ambush in Kamenica village (Kravica). "The situation on our lines is normal. "Captain Vaso Gujic." Does this document confirm the situation as it was on the ground in November 1992, that's to say that Poloznik and Pirici were under attack.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where from?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bjelovac, Kunjerac, Loznicka Rijeka, and Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now ask you to take a look at two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please give the witness these two documents. One document is dated 17 November 1992, bearing the number 04362980 and it's the Bratunac Brigade command document. The other one is also from the same command, the following day, 18 November 1992. 04362983.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look first at the document dated 17 November 1992 number 04362980. I will quote from a portion of the document. Item 1: "During the day" --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "During the night there were attempts by the enemy to pass through our lines in search of food. Their intentions were foiled." This is one document. Please take a look at the next document dated 18 November 1992 bearing the number 04362983. I'll read item 1 of the report for 18 November 1992, which says: "During the day the enemy was seen moving looking for food. One enemy soldier was captured in Voljavica village." In connection with these two documents, I wish to ask you the following: The situation, in terms of food, as far as you know in November 1992 in the Srebrenica area, was it so severe that people even crossed enemy lines in an attempt to find food?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was extremely difficult. The remaining stock of flour or whatever resources we had to produce flour were dwindling.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could these two documents be assigned a Defence exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want them together, Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we could treat them separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's the next number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D970, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have two documents being tendered. The first one consists of two pages, one in B/C/S, one in English, ERN 04362980 [Realtime transcript read in error "04362890"]. This is being marked as Defence Exhibit D970. The next document equally consists of two pages, one in B/C/S, one in English, ERN 04362983. This is being given Defence Exhibit Number D971.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 2980 for the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, 2980, yeah. Oh, I see. The transcript says "2890." It is 2980. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, at some point I'll go back to the issue of food but now I want to turn to something different. Generally speaking, based on your knowledge and experience, was the situation in Srebrenica and the surrounding villages getting exacerbated or not in the second half of November 1992, which was the subject of these two documents, that people were crossing enemy lines in search of food?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the presence of the Serb army in the area is concerned, was there a build-up of this presence in the period or not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a build-up of the military presence, but we don't know the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be handed a new document, please. This is a document by the Drina Corps command dated 18 November 1992, addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska entitled "formation of a manoeuvre unit," bearing the number 04292290 addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote from a part of the document. "The corps command has decided to form a brigade for exclusively manoeuvre purposes. It will be staffed with volunteers from our territory. We envisage that the commander be Lieutenant Colonel Svetozar Andric, whose present position will be filled by another commander. The following composition shall make the axis of the brigade: The commander, the command, a reconnaissance company, one infantry battalion, one tank company, one self-propelled artillery battery. In order to establish this unit as soon as possible, we would like to ask you to help in the following way: Secure a tank company, ten tanks, and ten personnel carriers from the Eastern Bosnian Corps." Witness, did you learn of the formation of such -- one such Serb unit at the time or later?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned this while listening to the news over the radio, because we had power -- we powered the radio by turning the pedals on a bike, and we heard about the establishment of this manoeuvre unit in Bratunac. Every day one could hear their reports from the battlefields over the radio, where they were boasting and exaggerating the successes of their units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just want to point your attention to the fact that the witness used the term "transistor," whereas the term "radio" was entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you listen to the information over the transistor or the radio?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the transistor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no objection. I merely suggest that a clarification should be sought. I am not quite sure what sort of news this is. "News" in English, of course, conveys information that's convoyed through mainstream media and there is also news that you can get from more, shall we say, exclusive sources, such as the Serb army itself. It's not apparent from this little bit of evidence what precisely the witness is speaking about and, in the context of this case, that could be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I definitely agree with you, Mr. Di Fazio. And Ms. Vidovic will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you said "I was listening to the news over the transistor," what sort of news were these?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb news.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were these Serb media, radio station, or --

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The -- so these were mass media?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that clarify the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Madam Vidovic, Judge Eser has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before we go on, I just wanted to ask: The news which the witness got from the radio or the transistor, however you may call it, how detailed was it? Did they bring all the details which you have saw -- seen in this exhibit or was it more a general news that something has been formed, without going into the details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the news were detailed. These were special programmes aimed at their groups, units, and their formation. These were programmes carrying information as to the composition and the formation of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. Madam Vidovic. We haven't given this document a number as yet. When you are ready, tender it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Could we please assign a number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. This document will become Defence Exhibit D972. It consists of two pages, one in B/C/S, one in English, ERN is 04292290.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know Svetozar Andric?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. Svetozar Andric was a professional soldier from the JNA, and in 1991 and 1992 on several occasions he attended meetings in Hotel Fontana. And I had that piece of information since I was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that this document mentions that the newly formed brigade will receive personnel on voluntary principle from our territory? Were you able to double-check or verify that later? Did you have any knowledge as to that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We confronted that unit in the Sase area as well as in Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was between the 12th and the 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the 12th," do you mean the 12th month of that year?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the Bratunac Brigade being formed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Via the Serb news, over the transistor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher now please put D766 in front of the witness. It is a document dated the 12th of December [as interpreted], 1992, report on the team visit of the Drina Corps, addressed to the Bratunac Brigade command. This is D766.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to quote but a portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is pointing out to me that, contrary to what appears on the transcript, the date is not 12th of December but 2nd of December, 1992 obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have before me the original in Bosnian and it states the 12th. I don't know what the English version mentions. Now I see. The English translation features the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I don't want to argue this, of course, but I'm not that sure that what appears before the first 2 in the third line, left-hand corner top of the page in B/C/S is a 1. I'm not quite sure, but anyway, I mean, I just wanted to alert you to the fact that in the English text it -- that figure seems to be longer than the other one which appears immediately after. It looks to me that it is a little bit longer. It's not the same, but I don't know -- let's move -- let's move. Let's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The date in itself is not important. This is what I thought was on the paper, but I wanted to ask something else from the witness. I wanted to quote a portion of the document around the middle of it. It states: "The Bratunac Light Brigade was formed on the 14th November 1992 in accordance with the envisaged establishment and was allotted its own operation. It was formed out of TO units in the main detachment and local commune units. The problems of its formation need to be analysed in greater detail."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hence my question: Did you have any knowledge -- did you acquire any information during December that the Bratunac Brigade was actually formed out of local population, from the Serb local communes?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because some of the soldiers that were killed I used to know. I knew that they were from Sase and Loznicka Rijeka and Andrici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I try not to dwell too long on any given document because the testimony will take too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Ms. Vidovic. We appreciate it. We'll have, incidentally, a break at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we show another document to the witness, D928. This is a Drina Corps command document dated the 24th of November, 1992, very urgent. Decision for further operations. Addressed to Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. I wanted to quote a part of item 22 pertaining to the Bratunac Brigade. It states that: "The Bratunac Brigade should use the main body of troops to launch an attack to break up enemy forces and reach the features of Loznik, Zanik, Caus, Bijela Stijena, use the remaining forces to cut the Srebrenica-Cerska road in coordination with part of the Birac Brigade, the Milici Battalion, and then in coordination with the Birac and Zvornik Brigades, liberate Pobudje, Hrnici and Konjevic Polje, thus creating conditions to open the Vlasenica-Milici-Drinjaca road. Consolidate the battalion as soon as possible and give it the task to penetrate as deep as possible into the area of Srebrenica, using the territory of Serbian villages and attack Srebrenica." As regards this document as well as the previous one, or, rather, the previous two you saw where we saw that the local Serb population was mentioned, I wanted to ask you the following: Is it correct, is it true, that the territory of Serb villages was used to carry out attacks against Srebrenica as well as other Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Loznicka Rijeka, Sikirica, Kunjerac, Kostanovice, Sase, Andrici -- rather, were these locations used to launch attacks, to attack the surrounding Muslim villages in November and December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In particular, the villages of Poloznik, Pirici, Pribici, Stozersko, and Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was artillery used from those areas to attack Srebrenica in that period?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having in mind those attacks and the degree of isolation of the Muslim villages that you mentioned yesterday, during November and December of 1992, was the situation becoming worse for the local Muslim population in Srebrenica and the villages you mentioned, making it unbearable?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the situation became unbearable. There were daily artillery and infantry attacks, ambushes were laid in the forests where people took refuge.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like concerning food in November and December of 1992 when it comes to the Muslim population of Podrinje, including the villages you mentioned? Perhaps we can now expand on what you started explaining just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was unbearable. The stocks were dwindling, the last remaining food we had disappeared, in particular in certain villages and now I have in mind whatever we could use to make flour, what was left of the wheat and corn, various roots of plants, as well as some apple, oats that was previously used only to feed cattle. And you can just about imagine what one such piece of bread would look like, making of ground oats and everything I mentioned. It is almost like a plaster food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I presume that you knew that a humanitarian convoy entered Srebrenica in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that, but that was much too little for tens of thousands of refugees in the town itself as well as thousands of refugees in the nearby forests.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I hear you correctly when you said that that was but a drop in the ocean for the local population?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your knowledge was the situation in Voljavica, Zaluzje, Biljaca, Prisoje, and Vejzovce particularly grave in those particular villages? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Those villages and the refugees from those villages were in an even graver situation. They used to have thousands of inhabitants and only a portion of the inhabitants could be accommodated in Srebrenica and its environs. The remainder of the population was to be found in large groups in the wider area of Voljevica, Zaluzje, Pirici, and there was total chaos, hunger, disease, and the shelling and infantry attacks were constant. People died of minor wounds and lacerations. They were virtually destroyed, both mentally and physically.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The groups of refugees you mentioned in particular, were they attacked during December 1992 from the Serb villages you mentioned Bjelovac, Sase, and Zaluzje?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is Loznicka Rijeka a part of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Loznicka Rijeka is attached to Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we now take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute -- we'll have a 30-minute break, starting from now. That means we'll reconvene at 4.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand either or both of you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I asked the witness be kept out. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you did the right thing if you need to address the -- what is it about? Who is going first? Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Looking at the transcript of the beginning of this session we have two very short questions. My first question is your Trial Chamber, Your Honours, have granted certification and the question, first question, is: Does that mean that Defence does not have to file a motion ex -- 73(B)? My second question is: By your grant of certification, does it also mean that in the opinion of this Trial Chamber, the Prosecution should not proceed on conducting an interview while this appeal is in progress?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would imagine you have got something to say about that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, I think it might save time if I raise my matters because it may supercede the two questions asked by Mr. Wubben. But just on the latter point, I think it's obvious that if the Prosecution were to interview the witness in the meantime the whole thing would be moot. No point in appealing. So that's -- to me is obvious. But in any event this may all be superceded by the following, Your Honour. During the -- during the sitting we were trying to contact the witness to see -- because he is travelling a long distance and what his plans are. And the fact is he is very shortly, today, in a matter of hours embarking on a plane for a ten-hour journey trip here. He's been planning for this trip for an extremely long time, so is the United States government, and particularly this witness. And the fact is, we want to keep good relations with that witness. We want to good relations with the United States government as well, and we really anticipate that if this poor man has to cancel all his plans at the last minute and stay in the United States and, you know, he has all sorts of other commitments, that we will lose a huge amount of goodwill. Secondly, as I mentioned before, Your Honour, the second witness we planned next week we do indeed have a sequence planned. There is a way his testimony fits in to the prior witness's testimony. We can't reschedule him because he's going to Malaysia. So it would disrupt everything. So in light of that, I wish to withdraw my application for certification and so, as a consequence of that, and I'm not saying we -- we're in any way happy with it or we agree with it, but the consequence is that -- that the Prosecution may go ahead and interview Lieutenant Dudley but without, as Your Honour has said, interfering with our schedule, our proofing schedule, and that schedule is a matter of public knowledge, practically. We filed it with the Victims and Witnesses section days ago and with the US government. And so it's clearly set on record. We're not coming up with a new proofing schedule now. It comprises Friday afternoon, Saturday, and Sunday. And, as Your Honour said, if the Prosecution has any difficulty in having an interview with Lieutenant Dudley outside that schedule, that's a matter for them. They should have dealt with this months ago, and nonetheless they would have an opportunity on Friday morning to interview him, provided also that we do have immediate disclosure of the list of topics so that we can recognise with the United States government, get permission to re-examine on those topics. And I'm sure if the United States government's permission is needed to disclose that list, I'm sure it will be forth coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, is there feedback from you or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. So, Your Honours, I take it that the witness will take the plane to Europe, as scheduled, tomorrow. We should be able and to try to organise the interview by Friday. As the court session will end at by a quarter to 2.00, I guess that is partly the beginning of the afternoon. We will seek for the opportunity to try to schedule it until the end of the proceeding on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is -- I don't think we are on the same wavelength. I think he is leaving today and arriving tomorrow and there is this six-hour -- we are depending on where he is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He's travelling today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether it is eastern --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, travelling today, arriving tomorrow. And our proofing schedule, I thought I was very clear, is Friday afternoon, we start interviewing him Friday afternoon. So it would be a question of someone from the Prosecution team and there are five prosecuting attorneys interviewing him in the morning, Friday morning. That's the only way it can avoid interfering with our schedule, our proofing schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned our requirement is just one, Mr. Wubben. How you schedule and when you schedule this with the US embassy here is none of our concern, except insofar as we required already both of you to ensure that the scheduling of your interview would not interfere with the scheduled proofing by the Defence, which now we know has been fixed for Friday afternoon. So what you need to do is make sure whoever will be dealing with that witness from the Prosecution side, I don't know who that is, will be available for interviewing him before the proofing by the Defence starts. So you have to arrange that with the US government -- with the US embassy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So indirect -- my question was -- because I already told the Trial Chamber that we will aim for Friday morning interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Indirectly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it is possible tomorrow afternoon, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We have to organise that. Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. But I also touched the fact that the morning session ends at a quarter to 2.00, so that's partly the beginning of the morning, and I wonder. So let me be very specific. If the Defence already start prior to a quarter to 2.00, meaning prior to the end of the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I see your point. What time are you starting? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was trying to find my email to the US government and to the VWS. Will you give me a moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Usher, please get the witness ready. Oh, he is out. I don't think he is very happy with us, this witness having to wait sometimes three-quarters of an hour, sometimes ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 2.00 till 4.00 on Friday. My apologies, 2.00 till 6.00 on Friday is what we've told the Victims and Witnesses Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking of a quarter of an hour, so basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will cooperate amongst -- between yourselves on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, both of you. Let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to put questions as directly as possible as to gain time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yet I will try not to lead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did your group and yourself participate in the fighting around Bjelovac around the 14th of December, 1992, until the 22nd of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present at any meeting when the Bjelovac action was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive an order by anyone to enter into combat?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were the leader of a group, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How come you went to the wider area of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a minute ago, the refugees from Voljavica and that area, not all of them could be accommodated in houses, but rather they went -- they were outside in large groups. One such group of about 60 was in a house of mine, and on several occasions they went out to look for food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the transcript does not reflect what the witness said. Now it seems clear --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said "60" refugees in your own house? You may continue.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those witnesses [as interpreted] went out looking for food into that area of Bjelovac, Biljaca, and Voljavica. On one such occasion they told me that the situation there is very serious, unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said those refugees went looking for food?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the refugees went looking for food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not witnesses went looking for food?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the refugees said that the situation was very grave? --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Let him go ahead with the question and we'll correct it. It's an evident mistake. It shouldn't be "witnesses went looking for food." Sometimes they do but ... Please, Madam, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received a message from someone that the situation there was very serious. Could you tell us who gave you that message.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Midhat Salihovic told me that. His group was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was his group?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His group was in the area of Luljaska [phoen], just above Voljavica and Biljaca and he originated from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the area of the Srebrenica or Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the area of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Midhat Salihovic a superior group leader to you in any regard?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally receive any task to go there and fight around Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whose decision was it then?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my personal decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you want to achieve?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to help those people. They were starved, and I wanted to change the situation. They were still out in the forest in large groups, and the only thing they wanted was to go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were those people trying to find some food?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know a group leader by the name of Hajro or a fighter called Hajro, pertaining your visit to Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew of no such a leader, of no one by the name of "Hajro."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean there was no such a person, at least not a prominent person in the area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The people who went with you, did they do this voluntarily or did you order it to them as a group leader?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They went voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you point out the area of Biljaca and Luljaska for the chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to see exactly where he -- okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Midhat Salihovic asked for your assistance. When did you set out precisely, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone lead you to that area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were led by a guy who was in my group as a refugee from the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you point it out on the map for the Chamber as to which route you took to the area where you met with Midhat Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you moved about, by foot, in some vehicles, or did you use horses, and which localities did you go through?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved on foot through the forest across Vitovci [phoen], Azici, in between Tri Kralja and Sase, towards Luljaska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the red you marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost I wanted to ask you the following: How many people did you set out with? How many were in your group?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were around 20 people in my group, and the remainder of the people were left behind to stay on the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of those 20, did you take any civilians with you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notify any civilians as to the fact that you were to go to the area of Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No matter where you went, was it your custom to notify civilians?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We wanted to do it as secretly as possible so that our route wouldn't be discovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that we wouldn't be discovered. Why is it? Why didn't you want the civilians to come along?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For various reasons. The larger the group, the more noticeable it is and moving about that territory a larger group would be easily detected from the Serb positions, thus initiating shelling right away, the consequence of which would be a great number of casualties among the civilians as well as the fighters who were on the move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day, the 14th of December, 1992, on your way between Tri Kralja and Azici, did you come across a large group of civilians?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At a certain moment when I turned around I saw a mass of people following us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you call them?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called them "torbari," sort of carpet-baggers. It was a special term we used. Those people would follow an armed group as soon as they would notice it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you try to do on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with five or six other men, I tried to ask them not to follow, but as it was in vain I started shouting and a small group obeyed but the rest remained in the forest or they left the road and later started following us again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do consequently?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed along that route between Tri Kralja and Sase towards Luljaska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: What were you armed with?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a few semi-automatic rifles as well as automatic rifles, a few hunting rifles, shotguns, a couple of makeshift guns, and two Zoljas captured in previous combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The semi-automatic and automatic rifles, how did you come to possess that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of it was seized by -- from the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you wear any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We wore civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, did any in your group have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never had any.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you set out, did you wear bands around your upper arm or around your head?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my group never wore ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain for the Chamber why is it that your group never wore ribbons?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the torbari assumed that they would notice somebody carrying a ribbon or a band, they would put it on as well and they would follow the fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why were they doing that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So as to move about more easily, because otherwise we would forbid them to accompany us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the group of Midhat Salihovic wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were wearing civilian clothing as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the area of Kunjerac -- or rather, did you at a certain point reach the area of Kunjerac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met with Midhat Salihovic and his group, and we came to the area of Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you came there, what did you see in terms of weaponry, equipment, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the approach to the area of Kunjerac, we realised that the entire area was mined. In between the houses and next to the houses themselves, there were mortars of large calibre, that is 120-millimetre, as well as a POT [as interpreted] or an anti-aircraft gun of 20-millimetre -- rather, 20/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber where those pieces were located in Kunjerac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to the houses themselves in Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a mortar would discharge, one could see a flash from the houses or, rather, next to the houses. And when they would open fire from the anti-aircraft gun, every 10th or 12th bullet was a tracer bullet to locate the target more easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Hence you were able to observe that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We observed that when they opened fire on the forest where refugees were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the houses in Kunjerac, did you see anything else?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the openings on the houses were actually turned into machine-gun nests. They used sandbags and other sort of material.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long were you at Kunjerac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fighting around Kunjerac lasted for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you were there throughout the two days?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the two days, were there any sorties by planes?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two planes and they came on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what the planes were doing? Were they dropping bombs or were they just flying about?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the planes threw bombs on parts of Poljic and Poloznik and the other one was dropping ammunition on Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe whether the plane targeted other areas except for Pirici, that's to say Loznicka Rijeka or other areas?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the general area of Loznicka Rijeka, Pirici, it was active in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said something that wasn't entered into the transcript. Did you say that a plane was dropping ammunition?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a plane which dropped on several occasions several crates of ammunition above Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These ammunition drops, were they helpful to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the houses in Kunjerac are placed on a -- quite a steep slope, as the ammunition crates were dropped they landed on the slope, rolling down towards us, which helped us in the course of combat. Had it not been for the ammunition, we would not have been able to seize Kunjerac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
